interactive.title: The turning arm
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens, all on one picture: axes drawn with the same scale both ways, and a circle of radius 1 round the centre. An arm of length 1 runs from the centre to the circle at angle θ, measured anticlockwise from pointing right. On the screens that show an idea you can drag the arm's tip round. Dashed lines drop from the tip to each axis, and each axis carries its own readout to three decimal places: cos θ along the across axis and sin θ up the up axis, each with its sign. Under the arm is lesson 1's right-angled triangle: the arm is its hypotenuse, 1 long, the side along the across axis is cos θ and the upright side is sin θ, because each ratio is that side divided by 1. As the arm passes into another quarter the triangle flips with it, and a side that lies left of the centre or below it is drawn dashed, because the coordinate it stands for is negative. A third readout adds the squares, cos² θ + sin² θ, and shows 1 at every angle, because the triangle is right-angled with a hypotenuse of 1, so Pythagoras applies; on an axis, where the triangle flattens, one square is 0 and the other 1. Screen 1 is lesson 1's triangle at 30°, its tip at (0.866, 0.5). Screen 3 turns the arm to 150°, where the tip is at (−0.866, 0.5). Screen 5 sweeps the arm through the four quarters, with each quarter's signs written inside it, stopping at 210° and 330°. Screen 7 shows the squares adding to 1 at 150°, 0.75 + 0.25, and the arm's slope, sin θ ÷ cos θ, which is tan θ: positive where sine and cosine share a sign, with no value at 90°, where the across is 0. Screen 9 adds a level line you drag up and down. Where it crosses the circle two arms are drawn with their angles, mirror images across the up axis, so at height 0.5 they are 30° and 150°, which add to 180°, and an arc on the left shows the 150° arm making the same 30° with the across axis; at the very top or bottom the two arms become one. Below the circle a calculator keys sin⁻¹ 0.5 and shows only 30°. Screen 12 asks for tan 210°, and once it is answered a faint arm at 30° shows the same slope on the same line. Until the cosine puzzles on screens 8 and 13 are answered, the triangle's sides are drawn plain, so the picture does not give the sign away. The other screens ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? draws the answer on the circle. A negative angle, such as the −30° the calculator gives for sin⁻¹(−0.5), is drawn turned clockwise, and lands on the same arm as 330°.
interactive.ignores: The circle has radius 1 in no particular unit, because sine and cosine are ratios of lengths; an arm of any other length scales both coordinates by its length. Readouts are rounded to three decimal places and angles to one, while the working keeps every figure. The arm is shown from 0° to 360°; turning on past a full turn, or clockwise below 0°, brings the same arm round again, which is how −30° and 330° are the same arm.

explain.text:
Lesson 1's ratios lived inside a right-angled triangle, so they stopped at 90°. Put that triangle on a turning arm and sine and cosine work for every angle, sometimes coming out negative. Draw axes as in The coordinate plane, with a circle of radius 1 round the centre. A full turn is 360°,[^1] and the angle θ is measured from an arm pointing right, along the across axis, turning anticlockwise; an angle turned that way counts as positive.[^2] Lay lesson 1's triangle under the arm with θ at the centre. The arm is the hypotenuse, the upright drop from the tip is the side opposite θ, and the stretch along the across axis is the side next to it. Sine is opposite ÷ hypotenuse and cosine adjacent ÷ hypotenuse,[^3] and here the hypotenuse is 1, so sin θ is simply the tip's height and cos θ is how far across the tip is. So the tip sits at the point (cos θ, sin θ):[^4] cosine across, sine up. At 30° that is (0.866, 0.5). A circle of radius 1 used this way is called the [[unit circle]].

Now turn the arm past 90° and keep the same rule: cos θ is the tip's across coordinate and sin θ its up coordinate, signs and all. Between 0° and 90° this gives lesson 1's values, and it needs no triangle to work, so beyond 90° it is how sine and cosine are defined, and it is what the calculator works out. At 150° the tip is 0.866 left of the centre and 0.5 up, so cos 150° = −0.866 and sin 150° = 0.5. The axes cut the circle into four quarters, called [[quadrant]]s, which this lesson numbers anticlockwise from the top right. In the first quadrant the tip is right and up, so both are positive. In the second it is left, so the cosine is negative. In the third it is left and down, so both are negative. In the fourth it is down, so the sine is negative. That is why sine, cosine and tangent are positive or negative depending on the quadrant.[^5] Tangent was opposite ÷ adjacent, and on the arm those sides are sin θ and cos θ, so tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ: the arm's slope, rise over run. It is positive where sine and cosine share a sign, in the first and third quadrants, and at 90° the run is 0, so tan 90° has no value, like the gradient of an upright line in Straight-line graphs. An angle between 180° and 360°, like 210° or 330°, is called a reflex angle;[^6] the arm treats it like any other.

Two more facts come straight from the picture. Off the axes, the arm is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose other sides are cos θ and sin θ, so Pythagoras gives cos² θ + sin² θ = 1, where sin² θ means (sin θ)². Squaring takes the signs away, so it holds in every quadrant: at 150°, 0.75 + 0.25 = 1. On an axis one is 0 and the other 1 or −1, so it holds there too. And a level line at height 0.5 crosses the circle twice, at 30° and at 150°, because the circle is the same on both sides of the up axis: mirror the 30° arm across it and you get the 150° arm, at the same height. So sin (180° − θ) = sin θ. Two angles that add up to 180°, like 30° and 150°, are called [[supplementary]].[^7] The calculator's sin⁻¹ gives only one angle, between −90° and 90°, so the second angle from 0° to 360° comes from the picture. For sin θ = 0.8, sin⁻¹ gives 53.1°, and the level line crosses again at 180° − 53.1° = 126.9°. This turning arm comes back in From circle to wave, where its height traced against time draws the wave of an AC supply. **On a turning arm of length 1 the tip is at (cos θ, sin θ),[^4] so sine and cosine have a value at every angle, positive or negative by quadrant.[^5]**

analogy.text: Turn the handle of a cable drum and its knob goes round a circle. Measured from the axle, the knob is so far across and so far up; over the top it moves to the other side of the axle, and round the far side it drops below the axle. Count right and up as positive, left and down as negative, and take the handle's angle anticlockwise from pointing right: the knob's two measurements, as fractions of the handle's length, are cos θ and sin θ. On the way round there are two places at each height, one either side of the axle, except at the very top and bottom, where there is one.
analogy.breaks: The knob's position comes round again every turn, so 30° and 390° put it in the same place, though the drum has wound on a whole turn more of cable, which the angle's sine and cosine cannot tell you.

practice.text:
- Picture the arm. Find the quadrant: 0° to 90° is the first, 90° to 180° the second, 180° to 270° the third, 270° to 360° the fourth.
- Read the signs from where the tip is: left of the centre, the cosine is negative; below it, the sine is negative.[^5]
- For a value, use the calculator in degrees mode;[^8] it gives the sign for you. Check the sign against the picture.
- To find every angle from 0° to 360° with a given sine, press sin⁻¹ for the first angle, then picture the level line at that height. It crosses the circle at that angle and at 180° minus it; at the very top or bottom the two are one angle. A negative first angle, such as −30°, is the same arm as 360° − 30° = 330°.
- Check each answer by taking its sine.

**Rule of thumb:** Cosine across, sine up. Two angles share a sine: θ and 180° − θ.

**Worked example:** Find every angle from 0° to 360° with sin θ = 0.3. sin⁻¹ 0.3 = 17.5°, in the first quadrant. The level line at 0.3 crosses the circle again in the second quadrant, at 180° − 17.5° = 162.5°. Keep the whole angle in the calculator and sin 162.5° gives 0.3 back. For sin θ = −0.3 the line is below the centre: sin⁻¹ gives −17.5°, the same arm as 360° − 17.5° = 342.5°, and its mirror image is 180° + 17.5° = 197.5°.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking the across coordinate as the sine.[^9] The sine is the height; the cosine is across.
- Stopping at the calculator's one angle. sin θ = 0.8 has two angles from 0° to 360°, 53.1° and 126.9°.
- Dropping the sign past 90°. cos 110° is −0.342, not 0.342, because the arm points left. The next lesson's cosine rule needs that minus sign.
- Using 360° − θ for the second angle with the same sine. That angle keeps the cosine and flips the sine: sin 306.9° is −0.8, not 0.8.
- Taking only the positive root from cos² θ + sin² θ = 1. When sin θ = 0.6, cos θ is 0.8 or −0.8, and the quadrant decides which.

interactive.title: The turning arm
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the arm's tip reading cos θ across and sin θ up, each turning negative in its own quarters while the two squares still add to 1, when you drag the arm round the circle.

checks.label: Angles are based on parts of a full turn, which is 360°: dragging the tip anywhere round the centre gives an angle from 0° up to but not including 360°, every quarter of the turn is reachable, and turning the arm on by a full 360° puts its tip back in the same place, so 30° and 390° are the same arm

The terminal side of the angle intersects the circle at the point (x, y), which is equivalent to (cos t, sin t): at whole angles all the way round, the arm's tip, measured off the drawing, lies on the circle, as far across as cos θ and as far up as sin θ, and the readout on each axis and the row under the picture give those same values

Sine is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse and cosine the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse: on the first screen the upright side opposite θ divided by the arm, the hypotenuse, both measured off the drawing, is what the up axis reads, the side along the across axis divided by the arm is what the across axis reads, and the arm is exactly as long as the circle's radius

Sine, cosine and tangent all have different positive or negative values depending on what quadrant they are in: at whole angles all the way round, a side of the triangle is drawn dashed exactly when the coordinate it stands for is negative, the readouts carry the same signs, the slope row's tangent is negative exactly where sine and cosine have different signs, and the signs written in each quadrant on the four-quadrant screen match the tip's signs there

Scientific calculators need to be used for trigonometry and should be in degrees mode: the calculator on the level-line screen is marked DEG at every height of the line, and its inverse sine gives the angle in degrees, the one an arm is drawn at, where radians would give a far smaller number

Other students incorrectly identified the x-coordinate as the sine ratio: the first puzzle offers the tip's across coordinate as a wrong answer, with its own hint and its own red working, and on every screen with readouts the sine sits on the up axis and the cosine on the across axis
cos² θ + sin² θ = 1 at every whole angle: the squares row always comes to 1, at 150° it reads 0.75 + 0.25 = 1, and on an axis one square is 0 and the other 1

tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ is the arm's slope, rise over run: at 150° the slope row reads 0.5 ÷ −0.866 = −0.577, at whole angles off the up axis it equals the drawn rise over run, and at 90° and 270°, where the run is 0, it says tan has no value

Two angles share each sine, mirror images across the up axis that add up to 180°: at every height of the level line from −1 to 1 each arm's tip lies on the circle and on the line, the calculator's angle lies between −90° and 90°, the row gives the second angle from it, at 0.5 the arms are at 30° and 150°, and at the very top and bottom the two arms are one

Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, every wrong answer has its own hint and its own red row of working, the answer appears once it is given, and before an answer nothing in the picture gives it away

No label sits on another label or a handle, or runs off the picture, on any screen in any state: puzzles answered right, wrong or with Why? open, the arm dragged all the way round, the level line at every height
Every demonstration has finished within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; each answer and Why? has settled within 1.8 s

applied.problem: "Sine, cosine and tangent change sign from one quadrant to the next" is false read literally (sine stays positive from the first to the second quadrant); and "the arm is always the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle" fails on the axes (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°), where the triangle flattens though the identity still holds.

A length is never negative: it is the coordinate a dashed side stands for that is negative; and the squares readout’s reason (a right-angled triangle) does not exist on the axes, where the triangle flattens, though the sum is still 1.
"Two places at each height" fails at the very top and bottom of the circle, where the knob has only one place at that height (the lesson itself says the two arms become one there).
